A federal judge blocked the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday from continuing a review of Disney’s local broadcast licenses for now, a blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to rein in national media organizations.

Judge Loren L. AliKhan of Federal District Court in Washington granted Disney, the parent company of ABC, the preliminary injunction it sought and denied the F.C.C.’s attempts to dismiss the suit.

The federal agency, which is run by a Trump appointee, Brendan Carr, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. ABC did not immediately respond to a request, either.

items.title: Trump Rejoiced in the Market’s Nvidia Surge. It Didn’t Last Long.
items.summary: The retreat of the stock market in recent days shows how President Trump’s push to reinstall the company’s chief executive has collided with the realities of his other policies.
items.full_text:
Title: Trump Rejoiced in the Market’s Nvidia Surge. It Didn’t Last Long. - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/25/us/politics/trump-nvidia-stock-market.html

Published Time: Thu, 26 Nov 2026 00:36:54 GMT

Markdown Content:
President Trump revels in his ability to move markets, no matter how fleeting.

Once it became clear that he had persuaded Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstall Jensen Huang as the company’s chief executive, [waving away the national security concerns](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/us/politics/trump-nvidia-national-security.html) about Mr. Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, he celebrated the stock surge that followed.

“Now it’s a rocket ship going in the right direction,” he exclaimed on CNBC soon after the news was announced on Monday morning and Nvidia stock surged more than 30 percent. Turning to one of his go-to phrases, he proclaimed: “It could be that there’s never been anything like it, actually.”

Perhaps there hasn’t. Or perhaps it was just temporary: Nvidia dropped 5.9 percent on Tuesday and another 5 percent on Wednesday, suggesting that at least some investors believe that Mr. Huang’s resignation and restoration — or the A.I. bubble it may help burst — might weigh on the company’s long-term prospects.

It is all a reminder that while markets may move temporarily, celebrating those gains as evidence of lasting economic success is risky business. In this case, the immediate boost from Nvidia’s surprise reversal appears to have been [undercut by the uncertainty](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/25/business/stocks-sp500-nvidia-ai.html) created by the fear of an A.I. bubble and Mr. Trump’s other interventions, including his disruption of international trade and the continuing, long-term market effects of his decision to go to war with Iran.

In his first term and again in his second, Mr. Trump has often cited stock market performance as proof that he is the master of the many intersections between the presidency and economic performance. But Mr. Trump has also made it clear that he does not subscribe to the theory that if a president is responsible for market surges, he must also be responsible for declines.

On Wednesday morning, as much of the country was trying to figure out how to get to their Thanksgiving celebrations, Mr. Trump was clearly looking for an explanation for why the Jensen Huang bump didn’t last more than a day. He settled on an explanation that he quickly relayed on his social media account: The markets had discovered that, three weeks prior, the country swept Democrats back to power.

“Stocks are down sharply because of the November Third Election results,” Mr. Trump wrote. “I wasn’t on the Ballot, but if I was, the results, just like all three times before, would have been much different, and the Stock Market, and your 401-k’s, would be BOOMING. I told you so!!!”

Mr. Trump may have forgotten that during the last weeks of the campaign, he urged voters to come out and “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” Exit polls suggest that many voters did just that.

Of course, all presidents want to take credit for economic success and deflect responsibility for bad news. But Mr. Trump takes this tendency a step further, embracing markets for instant validation of his decisions — whether on tariffs or Nvidia or going to war — and then seeks other explanations when the inevitable downturn raises the inevitable question of whether presidential responsibility is a two-way street.

The past 10 months have been littered with case studies of those risks.

Mr. Trump sounded supremely confident that his decision to attack Iran on Feb. 28 would result in minimal market disruption. Sure, there would be a surge in oil prices, and thus in gasoline, for a few weeks while the Iranian regime cracked apart. But then, he assured everyone, prices would fall and markets would surge as it became clear that new leaders there would be able to pump old oil wells.

On March 9, barely 10 days into the war, Mr. Trump waved aside a question about whether the United States would seize Iranian oil, and use it for both American enrichment and to drive down the market price. “Certainly people have talked about it,” he said. Soon after he repeatedly insisted that the war was over, that Iran had lost and that prices at the pump would decline.

Certainly, he said, they would be down by Labor Day.

They weren’t, and Vice President JD Vance gave an unsparing assessment of the result. “The reason we lost is the war,” he [declared in a social media post](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/vance-iran-war-midterms-trump.html) that followed the Republican loss of control over the House and the Senate.

Mr. Trump has occasionally tried to mitigate the fallout. He ordered up the purchase of Russian diesel oil, declaring that sanctions on Russia — rather than anything that was happening in the Persian Gulf — were responsible for the high cost of diesel fuel. It turns out that the Russian supply was so marginal, about a day’s consumption by the United States, that it made no difference on the market.

He has done the same with tariffs, arguing that foreign companies, not American diners, pay the price. (On Wednesday, the administration rolled out a slate of new tariffs targeting imports from dozens of countries.) Instead, the tariffs have helped fuel inflation, which [continued to rise](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/25/business/economy/inflation-pce-interest-rates.html) in October, according to a key measurement. And inflation has forced the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates — exactly the opposite of the market reaction Mr. Trump predicted.

But he remains determined to look to the Dow Jones and the Nasdaq to reinforce the wisdom of his decision making. “The stock is up,” he [marveled to The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/us/politics/trump-nvidia-huang.html) about Nvidia after detailing his success in persuading the board that American “geniuses” like Mr. Huang needed to be forgiven for their mistakes, so that they could continue to innovate.

In the end, he told another interviewer, the markets would show that Mr. Huang’s return was a “net positive.”

The stock closed for the Thanksgiving holiday at $149, down around $100 from its high at the beginning of October.

items.title: A Rumored $300 Million Score on Nvidia’s Stock Surge Isn’t Backed by Trading Records
items.summary: Three data providers say they have no evidence to support the online claim that insider trading generated a 9,000 percent return.
items.full_text:
Title: A Rumored $300 Million Score on Nvidia’s Stock Surge Isn’t Backed by Trading Records - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/25/business/nvidia-stock-insider-trading-rumor.html

Published Time: Thu, 26 Nov 2026 01:03:27 GMT

Markdown Content:
Shortly after news of Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief executive sent the company’s stock price surging on Monday, rumors began circulating on social media about a seemingly suspicious trade that made huge profits on an unlikely outcome.

“This is INSANE,” said an account on X, which, according to its bio, is run by a stock and options trader. The post claimed that someone had bought $3.4 million worth of Nvidia options on Friday, which resulted in a profit of $312 million, a gain of roughly 9,000 percent.

The claims were then shared almost 5,000 times and viewed by millions of people, according to X.

But three firms that track options activity said they had no evidence that the trade happened. And two said the size of the purported trade was so large that it was nearly impossible.

The extraordinary situation at Nvidia, in which members of the Trump administration [pushed board members](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/us/politics/trump-nvidia-huang.html) over the weekend to help pave the way for Mr. Huang’s return, raised suspicions broadly about whether anyone may have benefited financially from early knowledge of his reinstatement.

But the questionable post highlights how misinformation, long a problem in politics, can also spread within financial markets, adding to distrust of institutions amid broad concerns about corruption.

At the heart of the post is options trading, which allows investors to bet on a company’s future stock price.

Options, broadly, come in two types. There are “put” options, which give the buyer the right to sell a stock or an index at a prearranged price, and there are “call” options, which give the buyer the right to buy, also at a set price.

In each case, the buyer pays a fee, or premium, to own that right, with that premium rising and falling with the likelihood that the agreed-upon price will be reached before the options contract expires.

On X, the claim was that someone bought $3.4 million worth of call options on Friday that expired on Monday with a “strike price” of $160. The value of the options contracts rose alongside Nvidia’s stock price surge on Monday morning, netting an enormous profit. But there is no evidence that this trade ever took place.

Less than $100,000 worth of call options matching those parameters — a strike price of $160, expiring on Nov. 23 — were traded throughout the entire day on Friday, according to Unusual Whales and Market Chameleon, two firms that track such trades. The Options Price Reporting Authority, which collects trade data from all U.S. options exchanges, also found no evidence of the trade described.

The rise in the value of the contracts was roughly 9,000 percent, according to Market Chameleon’s data, lending credence to the claim. But even if one buyer owned every reported contract, the total value would have been closer to $8 million than over $300 million, it said.

When reached on X via direct message, the account that appeared to have initially posted the claim, @MrMikeInvesting, did not confirm the veracity of his post, nor did it provide evidence of the trade cited. The account responded that “some websites heavily filter the data they display.”

The account is among a number on social media that sell subscription services for trading tips, often accompanied by lofty claims of helping subscribers get rich, with disclaimers that what they provide is not financial advice subject to regulatory oversight.

X users can pay $9.99 per month to subscribe to the X account to gain access to subscriber-only posts. The account also directs users to another subscription platform called Whop, which offers services costing from $79.99 per month to a flat fee of $1,995 for a lifetime membership to investing content.

“I’m not a financial advisor,” the X account adds on its bio.
